name: Queenstown
tagline: Bungy, alpine lakes and Pinot Noir in the adventure capital
description:
Queenstown sits on the shore of a vast, lightning-bolt-shaped lake, hemmed in by jagged peaks with names like the Remarkables, and it wears its reputation as the world's adventure capital with a grin. This is where commercial bungy jumping began, where jetboats spin through narrow canyons and where paragliders drift past the gondola on almost every clear day.

Yet the town is as much about beauty as adrenaline. Walk the lakeside gardens at dawn, cross Lake Wakatipu on a century-old steamship or drive the road to Glenorchy, where every bend reveals scenery straight out of Middle-earth. Historic Arrowtown, a gold-rush village of stone cottages, glows with golden poplars each autumn, while the wineries of the Gibbston Valley pour some of the world's finest Pinot Noir. Milford Sound, with its sheer cliffs and thundering waterfalls, makes an unforgettable day trip.

Winter turns Queenstown into a ski town, with two major ski areas a short drive away, while summer brings long evenings, tramping trails and bracing lake swims. After dark, the compact center buzzes with bars, craft breweries and lakefront restaurants. Book activities early in peak season, pack for four seasons in a day and leave room for an unplanned adventure.

safety.notes: Crime is very low; the real risks are fast-changing alpine weather, icy winter roads and the adventure activities themselves. Check forecasts, carry layers on every hike and take your time driving on the left on winding mountain roads.

tipping: Tipping isn't expected in New Zealand, but rounding up or leaving about 10% for outstanding service at restaurants or on guided trips is always appreciated.
gettingAround: The compact center is easy to walk, and cheap flat-fare buses link the airport, Frankton, Arthurs Point and Arrowtown. For Glenorchy, Milford Sound and the wineries, rent a car or join a tour, as roads are winding and the weather changes quickly.
tips: Weather cancels flights, cruises and jumps regularly, so book adventure activities with flexible terms and keep a spare day in your plans.
The road to Milford Sound takes around four hours each way and can close in winter due to avalanche risk; a scenic fly-cruise saves the drive if budget allows.
Local buses charge a flat NZ$2 fare with a Bee Card, making trips to Arrowtown, Frankton and the airport very cheap.
Pack strong insect repellent for Milford Sound and Glenorchy, where tiny biting sandflies are relentless.
The UV here is fierce even on cool days, so wear sunscreen and sunglasses, especially on the snow and the lake.
Rent a bike and ride the Queenstown Trail to Arrowtown or the Gibbston wineries, with a shuttle back if the tastings get generous.
etiquette: Kiwis often thank the bus driver as they get off; join in.
Avoid sitting on tables or putting hats on food surfaces, which is considered culturally inappropriate in Māori tradition.
Stay on marked tracks, take your rubbish with you and give wildlife and livestock plenty of space.
Locals are relaxed and modest, so friendly first-name chat goes further than boasting about your adventures.

phrases.pronunciation: "Meet at the gondola at ten?" "Sweet as."
"There were heaps of people on the luge."
"Chuck your jandals on, we're going to the lake."
"Fill the chilly bin for the picnic."

phrases.english: A polite way of saying no

neighborhoods.name: Queenstown Central
neighborhoods.blurb: The walkable lakefront core of bars, restaurants, adventure booking offices and the Steamer Wharf, with the gondola just uphill.

neighborhoods.name: Fernhill
neighborhoods.blurb: A hillside suburb west of town with some of the best lake views, quiet motels and forest trails leading straight into the hills.

neighborhoods.name: Frankton
neighborhoods.blurb: The practical hub near the airport, with supermarkets, lakeside walking tracks and easy access to the ski fields.

neighborhoods.name: Arthurs Point
neighborhoods.blurb: A small village perched above the Shotover River canyon, handy for jetboating, hot pools and Coronet Peak.

neighborhoods.name: Kelvin Heights
neighborhoods.blurb: A peaceful peninsula across the Frankton Arm, lined with lakefront homes, a golf course and sunny walking paths.

dishes.name: Blue cod and chips
dishes.description: Flaky southern blue cod in crisp beer batter with thick-cut chips, wrapped in paper and eaten by the lake.

dishes.name: Mince and cheese pie
dishes.description: New Zealand's favorite hand-held meal: a flaky pastry case filled with rich minced beef gravy and melted cheese.

dishes.name: Central Otago Pinot Noir
dishes.description: The region's celebrated red wine, silky and full of dark cherry and spice, grown in the world's southernmost commercial wine region.

dishes.name: Pavlova
dishes.description: A crisp-shelled, marshmallowy meringue piled with whipped cream and fresh fruit, a proudly contested Kiwi classic.

dishes.name: Hokey pokey ice cream
dishes.description: Vanilla ice cream studded with crunchy golden nuggets of honeycomb toffee, a beloved New Zealand flavor.

events.name: Arrowtown Autumn Festival
events.description: Arrowtown celebrates its gold-rush heritage amid blazing autumn colors with a parade, street market, live music and gold-panning contests.

events.name: Queenstown Winter Festival
events.description: Held since 1975, this festival kicks off the ski season with fireworks over the lake, live music, comedy and wacky on-snow competitions.

events.name: Queenstown Marathon
events.description: Thousands of runners follow a spectacular course past lakes, rivers and Arrowtown to a lakeside finish in Queenstown.

attractions.name: Skyline Queenstown
attractions.description: A steep gondola ride whisks you about 450 meters above town to Bob's Peak, where the view over Lake Wakatipu and the Remarkables graces half the country's postcards. Stay to race down the luge tracks or watch paragliders launch off the slope.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy a gondola-and-luge combo online for a discount and ride up about an hour before sunset.

attractions.name: Queenstown Gardens
attractions.description: A peninsula of century-old trees, rose beds and lakeside paths poking out into Lake Wakatipu just steps from town. Locals play disc golf among the pines, and an ice rink and skate park keep kids busy.
attractions.bookingTip: Walk the peninsula loop at sunrise, when the lake is glassy and the Remarkables glow pink.

attractions.name: TSS Earnslaw
attractions.description: Launched in 1912, this coal-fired steamer still chugs across Lake Wakatipu trailing smoke from her red funnel, with the engine room open so passengers can watch the stokers at work. The crossing to Walter Peak high-country farm adds sheep-shearing demonstrations and a lakeside barbecue.
attractions.bookingTip: Book the farm-tour or barbecue combo if you have time, and claim an outdoor seat on the upper deck.

attractions.name: Arrowtown
attractions.description: This 1860s gold-rush village of schist cottages and timber shopfronts sits at the foot of the hills 20 minutes from Queenstown, its avenue of trees blazing gold in autumn. Try panning in the Arrow River and explore the restored huts of the old Chinese miners' settlement.
attractions.bookingTip: Take the cheap local bus from Queenstown or cycle the trail, and visit in late April for peak autumn color.

attractions.name: Kawarau Gorge Suspension Bridge
attractions.description: The world's first commercial bungy site opened in 1988 on this 1880 bridge over an emerald river gorge, and jumpers still plunge 43 meters toward the water, some dunking head first. Even if you don't jump, watching from the viewing decks is a heart-in-mouth spectacle.
attractions.bookingTip: Watching is free; jumps cost around US$170 and should be booked a few days ahead in summer.

attractions.name: Milford Sound
attractions.description: Sheer granite walls rise more than a kilometer straight out of the dark water of this fiord, streaming with waterfalls after rain while fur seals lounge on the rocks and dolphins ride the bow waves. Even the long drive from Queenstown through the Homer Tunnel is spectacular.
attractions.bookingTip: Rainy days are secretly the best, when hundreds of temporary waterfalls appear; bring sandfly repellent and check winter road closures.

attractions.name: The Remarkables
attractions.description: The serrated range that forms Queenstown's dramatic backdrop hosts a family-friendly ski field in winter, with terrain parks and gentle beginner slopes. In summer, the access road leads to an easy alpine walk to the tarn of Lake Alta.
attractions.hours: Ski season mid-June to early October, lifts about 09:00–16:00
attractions.bookingTip: Buy lift passes online in advance for lower prices and ride the ski shuttle from town, as road parking fills early.

attractions.name: Glenorchy
attractions.description: A tiny settlement at the head of Lake Wakatipu, reached by one of the world's most beautiful lakeside drives, surrounded by snowy peaks, braided rivers and beech forests that starred in the Lord of the Rings films. It's the gateway to the Routeburn Track, horse treks and kayak trips.
attractions.bookingTip: Stop at the Bennetts Bluff lookout on the way, and photograph the red wharf shed in Glenorchy at golden hour.

attractions.name: Queenstown Hill
attractions.description: A steady climb through pine forest from the edge of town leads to the Basket of Dreams sculpture and a sweeping view over lake, town and mountains. It takes two to three hours return and is far quieter than the gondola viewpoint.
attractions.bookingTip: Start from the trailhead on Belfast Terrace early in the morning, carrying water and a windproof layer.

attractions.name: Shotover River
attractions.description: Once one of the richest gold-bearing rivers on Earth, the Shotover now roars through narrow schist canyons where jetboats skim within inches of the rock walls. The historic bridge at Arthurs Point makes a thrilling free vantage point.
attractions.bookingTip: Jetboat rides run year-round but sell out on summer afternoons, so book a morning slot a day or two ahead.

hotels.name: Glacier Pine Lodge
hotels.description: A lakefront lodge of stone, glass and native timber with just 18 suites, each with a fireplace and a deck gazing across the water to the Remarkables. The spa's cedar hot tubs sit right above the lake.

hotels.name: Miner's Lantern Inn
hotels.description: A cluster of restored 1870s miners' cottages with schist walls, clawfoot tubs and wood-burning stoves, set around a garden of apple trees. The main street's cafés and the Arrow River trails are right at the gate.

hotels.name: Kea Loft Backpackers
hotels.description: A lively hostel steps from the gondola base, with pod-style bunks, a huge drying room for ski gear and a rooftop deck overlooking the lake. The activity desk scores backpacker discounts on jetboats and bungy.

hotels.name: Schist & Timber Hotel
hotels.description: Local schist, blackened timber and floor-to-ceiling glass make this lakefront hotel feel like a sleek modern alpine hut. Rooms have heated floors and deep baths, and the ground-floor bar pours only Central Otago wines.

hotels.name: Alpine Lookout Apartments
hotels.description: Two- and three-bedroom apartments on the slopes above town, with full kitchens, laundry and balconies overlooking the lake. They suit families and ski groups, with a bus stop right outside.

hotels.name: Head of the Lake Retreat
hotels.description: Solar-powered eco cabins scattered through the tussock outside Glenorchy, each with an outdoor bathtub beneath some of the darkest skies in the region. The lodge arranges horse treks, kayaks and guided walks on the Routeburn.

restaurants.name: Wharfside Chippy
restaurants.description: A takeaway window by the wharf frying beer-battered blue cod, crisp chips and kūmara wedges wrapped in paper. Eat on the lakefront steps as the steamer comes in, and guard your chips from the gulls.

restaurants.name: Hillside Flat White Co.
restaurants.description: A sunny corner café pulling expert flat whites for skiers and trampers, with a cabinet piled high with scones and slices and hearty brunch plates. The corn fritters with bacon and avocado are the local favorite.
restaurants.signatureDish: Corn fritters with bacon, avocado and tomato relish

restaurants.name: Tussock & Thyme
restaurants.description: A converted stone woolshed where the tasting menu follows the high country through the seasons, from wild thyme and venison to foraged mushrooms and Central Otago cherries. The cellar holds rare back vintages from Gibbston and Bannockburn.
restaurants.signatureDish: Lamb loin with wild thyme, smoked kūmara and cherry jus

restaurants.name: Fiordland Crayfish House
restaurants.description: A lakeside dining room showcasing southern seafood: Fiordland crayfish grilled with garlic butter, briny Bluff oysters in season and hot-smoked alpine salmon. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame the Remarkables at sunset.
restaurants.signatureDish: Grilled Fiordland crayfish with garlic butter

restaurants.name: Gorge Road Cellar Kitchen
restaurants.description: A cellar-door restaurant among the vines, where long lunches of venison, cheese boards and wood-fired bread are paired with estate Pinot Noir. Terrace tables look up the rocky gorge.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pinot noir-braised venison with parsnip purée

restaurants.name: Izakaya Yukiyama
restaurants.description: A snug, lantern-lit izakaya serving charcoal-grilled yakitori, crisp karaage and steaming bowls of miso ramen that hit the spot after a day on the slopes. The sake list favors small brewers, and the kitchen stays open late.

restaurants.name: Canyon Edge Tavern
restaurants.description: A timber-and-schist pub perched above the Shotover canyon, with a roaring fire, local craft beer on tap and hearty plates of lamb shank and blue cod. The deck is the place to be on long summer evenings.
restaurants.signatureDish: Slow-braised lamb shank with kūmara mash

restaurants.name: Mountain Road Bakehouse
restaurants.description: A tiny roadside bakery turning out flaky mince-and-cheese pies, venison pies and sticky caramel slices for trampers heading to the Routeburn. Grab a pie and a flat white and eat on the wharf.

experiences.name: Wild Water Canyon Jetboat Ride
experiences.description: Rocket through narrow schist canyons at up to 85 km/h, skimming past rock walls and spinning 360 degrees in a burst of spray. Waterproof jackets are provided, but expect to get a little wet.

experiences.name: Milford Sound Fly, Cruise & Fly
experiences.description: Soar over glaciers and hidden alpine lakes on a small-plane scenic flight, land at Milford's tiny airstrip and cruise the fiord to the Tasman Sea before flying back. It turns an eight-hour round-trip drive into a half-day of jaw-dropping views.

experiences.name: Gibbston Pinot Cellar Door Trail
experiences.description: Visit four boutique wineries in the Gibbston Valley with a wine-educator guide, tasting celebrated Pinot Noir, crisp Riesling and aromatic whites. The day includes a platter lunch among the vines and a stop to watch the bungy jumpers.

experiences.name: Lakeside Sauna & Glacial Plunge
experiences.description: Warm up in a wood-fired cedar sauna on the edge of Lake Wakatipu, then dare yourself into the snow-fed water before retreating to the heat. Sessions end with herbal tea and blankets as the mountains turn pink.
